newsitem.title: KAZAKHSTAN: Kazakh government says economy growing steadily.
newsitem.headline: Kazakh government says economy growing steadily.

text.p: Kazakhstan said on Friday its economy was now growing steadily, with gross domestic product (GDP) likely to rise 1.5 percent in the first half of this year.
"GDP is expected to grow by 1.5 percent in the first half of this year, compared to the same period last year," President Nursultan Nazarbayev told a cabinet meeting.
"Changes to the better are obvious," he said.
Dyusenbai Dyuisenov, deputy prime minister in charge of industry, told the meeting industrial output in the former Soviet republic would grow 2.7 percent over the same period.

Dyuisenov said the rise would be largely due to the revival of the Central Asian state's important oil-extacting, ferrous and non-ferrous metals industries, forecast to grow in the first half of this year by 17.1, 13.9 and 3.6 percent respectively.

The government expects the GDP of the resource-rich country -- five times the size of France but with a population of just 16.7 million people -- was expected to grow this year by two percent, compared to last year's 1.1 percent, he said.
Industrial production would grow by three percent, compared to last year's moderate 0.3 percent.
Last year was Kazakhstan's first year of economic growth since the launch of market reforms in 1992.
Nazarbayev said low inflation was another achievement.
He said consumer prices in the first five months of this year grew by 5.9 percent.
"In the first two weeks of June we registered deflation of 0.2 percent," he said, noting that the initial inflation target for June-January of this year was 9.3 percent.
Officials have said previously inflation could fall this year below the target of 17 percent. Consumer prices grew by 28.7 percent last year.
But the tough transition to a market economy has hurt many people in the Central Asian state.
Labour and Social Protection Minister Natalya Korzhova said that debts on salaries exceed 47 billion tenge, while pension arrears total another 36 billion tenge.
Four percent of the country's workforce are officially stated as unemployed, while hidden unemployment accounts for another 4.4 percent, she said.
"The demand for work is five times larger than the number of jobs available," Korzhova added.
